subject: Quantile of the posterior predictive distribution of the response variable

messages.author: 93f93e99d1eec3f2
messages.subject: Quantile of the posterior predictive distribution of the response variable
parts:
Dear Help,

 I am using INLA to fit a model of the negative binomial family with log-link to some time series. My goal is to obtain a quantile of the predictive posterior distribution of the response variable y_t.

My current code works but I wonder if I could make it faster.

Right now, after I have fit the model using INLA, I compute the quantile through Monte Carlo sampling. I draw random samples (inla.rmarginal) from the marginal for the mean of the negative binomial distribution (marginals.fitted.values) and for the overdispersion parameter theta (internal.marginals.hyperpar[[1]]). I draw mc.mutheta values of the mean and of the parameter theta. This gives me mc.mutheta (mean,theta)_j. For each of them I draw mc.y values from the negative binomial distribution parameterized by (mean,theta)_j. Thus I get a vector of mc.mutheta*mc.y values for the response, upon which I apply the quantile() function to get the quantile of the posterior predictive distribution I want. This is quite compute-intensive.

Therefore my question use: is there a faster way in INLA to get the quantile of the predictive posterior distribution of the response variable or to sample from this distribution?

Thanks a lot in advance!

Best wishes

Maëlle.

You're almost there, as you do not account for the dependence of the
overdispersion parameter and the fitted.values, but I guess its almost
right.

if you want to sample from the joint, then look at

inla.posterior.sample

which needs a result-object r=
inla(...,control.compute=list(config=TRUE)))

just make sure that the fitted.values are computed with the correct link
function (see the FAQ entry on the r-inla.org page).


Best
H


--

I'm new to INLA so I was hoping I could post a follow up to better understand inla.posterior.sample. I have a model with fixed effects, temporal autocorrelation (AR1 model), and spatial autocorrelation (Besag model). I have 2900 "observations" in my data (some are NAs for predictive purposes). The latent posterior samples for my model have 2900 "Predictor.xxxx" samples, 2900 "ID.xxxx" samples, and 2900 "year.xxxx" samples, where ID and year are the replicates for the AR1 and Besag models, respectively, plus the coefficients for the intercept and covariate for the fixed effects.

Are the "Predictor.xxxx" samples the "fitted values" from the joint posterior and the "ID.xxxx" and "year.xxxx" the estimated error for their respective models?

Adam

Sorry for the late reply, your email got lost...

Predictor.xxxx is the linear predictor and ID.xxxx and year.xxxx refers
to the model components f(ID,...) and f(year,...). The fitted values are
not simulated (you have to compute them 'manually' if required).
